title: UK’s first railway station wine to be produced
summary:
Denmark Hill rail station in south London will next year release its first vintage, made from Bacchus vines grown mere metres from the train tracks.

The post UK’s first railway station wine to be produced appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Denmark Hill rail station in south London will next year release its first vintage, made from Bacchus vines grown mere metres from the train tracks. Sarah Neish reports. Denmark Hill in Camberwell is about to become the first British railway station to produce a wine from vines grown on its property. The 30 Bacchus vines, planted by the Camberwell Society just metres away from the rail tracks, have yielded enough grapes to make 'Chateau Denmark Hill's' first vintage, a white wine, expected to be ready to drink by next year.

Community project

According to the Society's web page, it was awarded a grant in November 2020 and a Community Licence by Network Rail "to care for and develop the non-passenger areas at Denmark Hill station." As part of this endeavour, Society members have cleared "obscuring brush" in order to plant more than 10,000 bluebell and poppy seeds, alongside 1,500 crocus, grape hyacinth and daffodil bulbs. Additionally, members chose to create a vineyard housing 22 Bacchus vines, which sits near to "a mini tableau of Provence" in the form of 56 lavender plants. Winemaker Nick Mair confirmed to db: "We are expecting our first proper harvest this year." He added that while Bacchus is a "very forgiving" grape variety, the viticultural endeavour had not been easy, explaining that he and fellow winemaker Tony Coleman "had to remove bindweed from the slope, terrace it and then dig in holes for the vertical posts – a fair amount of work with no electricity or mechanised agricultural tools available." The Society added on an Instagram post that "the dream of sipping a glass of wine, grown right here in Camberwell, is becoming a reality... making history as we work on the first ever vineyard in a UK station." It is not yet known whether the wine will be sold to commuters, or kept for the consumption of the Society's own members, but given the tiny size of the vineyard and "very small-scale affair" described to db by Mair, bottles are expected to be limited. 

Why Bacchus?

Bacchus is gaining a reputation as England’s signature aromatic white grape variety, sometimes hailed as the "English Sauvignon Blanc" for its crisp acidity, and vibrant citrus notes. Created in Germany in 1933, Bacchus is a cross of Silvaner, Riesling, and Müller-Thurgau, and thrives in the relatively cool climate of English vineyards. It is also fairly hardy against damp and rainy conditions, another boon for English plantings. It is the fourth most planted grape variety in England (behind Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Pinot Meunier) and accounts for roughly 7% to 8% of total land under vine in the UK, with around 324 to 334 hectares planted. Furthermore, its commercial potential is also on the up as according to a report by industry body WineGB, Bacchus vines yielded especially well last year, producing 9.5 tonnes per hectare compared to its five-year average of just 6.75 t/ha.

title: Two Tribes rebrands, invests for growth and doubles down on the indie beer scene
summary:
London brewery Two Tribes has revealed a new identity for its core range alongside plans for expansion via the independent pubs and bars that helped to build the beer brand. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Two Tribes rebrands, invests for growth and doubles down on the indie beer scene appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
London brewery Two Tribes has revealed a new identity for its core range alongside plans for expansion via the independent pubs and bars that helped to build the beer brand. Jessica Mason reports. According to the brewery, its relaunch comes as “a deliberate statement of confidence”. In fact, it insisted that “while much of the independent beer sector is contracting under rising costs, Two Tribes is investing in its brand”. Founded in 2017 by veterans of the 90s club scene, the brewery has since grown from a King's Cross start-up into one of the capital's most distinctive independent names. Two Tribes beers also proudly carry SIBA's Indie Beer mark: the industry stamp that tells drinkers a beer comes from a genuinely independent UK brewery, not a brand owned by a larger holding group.

'Demand is clearly there'

Speaking to the drinks business, Two Tribes commercial director, Aaron Duffett said: “Independent brewers are being squeezed out of pubs by the global giants right now, and we think that's exactly the moment to plant our flag even further, rather than retreat.” Duffett explained to db that people want to buy independent beer, so “the demand is clearly there” and highlighted that “recent CAMRA figures show demand is 280% higher than independent beer's actual share of the pub market, yet we're the ones being crowded off the bar”. The rebrand lands against a tough backdrop for independent beer. SIBA's UK Brewery Tracker recorded 137 brewery closures across the UK in 2025 - a net rate of almost three a week, and a sharp rise on the year before. Yet demand for the beer itself remains strong: while overall UK beer volumes fell 1.8%, SIBA's independent members grew median volumes by 14%, and 89% of drinkers say they want independent brands stocked alongside global names.

'We're investing in the brand and backing the independent pubs and bars that built us'

"This is a moment of real confidence for us," said Duffett. "With hospitality costs rising and some brewers scaling back, we're doing the opposite. We're investing in the brand and backing the independent pubs and bars that built us. We're seeing drinkers move away from the big established craft names towards independent, local brands they can trust, and that demand is exactly where we want to meet them. Be it at the bar or on the shelf, we do so on our own merits, without a global brewer's budget behind it." The new identity, developed in collaboration with design studio All Purpose, replaces Two Tribes' previous look with a bolder visual world built around the brewery's new brand platform: Brewing Wonder.

'We've gone bold'

All Purpose co-founder and creative director Ted Heffernan said: "Two Tribes already had the substance, being one of London’s most loved independent breweries. The identity reinterprets the visual language and typographic vernacular of classic beer labels. We wanted to play with this familiarity, each beer took on its own identity through custom typography, colour and a shape-driven graphic system. We’ve gone bold, an identity designed to hold its own alongside big names in beer, while still feeling unmistakably premium and independent.” The relaunch keeps the beer exactly the same, but spans the full core range: Campfire (hazy IPA), Dream (pale ale) and Super Deluxe formerly known as Classic Lager (helles-style lager).

'They now look as fresh as they taste'

Two Tribes head brewer Francesco Mayell explained: "Campfire, Dream and Super Deluxe are the same beers people already know and love; what's changed is they now look as fresh as they taste. We've spent years getting the liquid right, and ensuring every keg and can that leaves the brewery has our seal of approval. From brewing through to packaging, we check every batch against 18 quality parameters, guaranteeing every brew is the best it should be." With its rebrand, Two Tribes re-emphasised that its brewery taproom “doubles as a home for music, food and events, and a place the brand uses to give culture a platform”. Inspired by the founders' roots in 90s club culture, Two Tribes also runs a regular DJ programme with King's Cross community station Voices Radio in a partnership that includes a free workshop series aimed at opening up DJing to people that have historically been underrepresented in the music industry.

'The start of our next chapter'

Two Tribes marketing director Thom Bradley reiterated that "Two Tribes has never just been about what's in the can. From the start we've wanted to be a platform for culture, somewhere music, creativity and people come together.” Duffett told db: “We’re a genuinely independent brewer from Kings Cross that can stand shoulder to shoulder with the biggest names on the bar. It's the start of our next chapter, and we think it's the most exciting one yet." The new-look core range is available on draught at the Two Tribes brewery tap location in King’s Cross which is named Campfire, The Standard London, The Royal Opera House, Urban Pubs & Bars, Inda Pubs and other independent pubs. In packaged format it can also be found in Sainsbury’s, M&S, Waitrose and Tesco stores and retails from around £2.50 per can.

title: Beyond Shadows tells the story of Luján de Cuyo
summary:
Beyond Shadows, the new wine from Doña Paula, pays tribute to Luján de Cuyo. Its eye-catching label suggests the story of the high-altitude Mendoza sub-region, where long histories meet innovative winemaking.

The post Beyond Shadows tells the story of Luján de Cuyo appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Beyond Shadows, the new wine from Doña Paula, pays tribute to Luján de Cuyo. Its eye-catching label suggests the story of the high-altitude Mendoza sub-region, where long histories meet innovative winemaking. Whether you first see two girls innocently playing or the chalky image of a skull, Beyond Shadows – Doña Paula’s new Argentine wine – certainly makes an impression. The label grabs the attention, and has been designed to tell the story of Luján de Cuyo. As a longstanding centre for high-quality Mendoza winemaking, the sub-region has generations of history. The skull represents the buried histories and forgotten practices that have made it great. It is a tribute to generations who have tended vineyards and built its name, and a recognition of the past buried in every vineyard. The two girls, meanwhile, represent the excitement and hope around Luján de Cuyo’s continuing prestige. Moreover, they symbolise the visible bounty seen in the vineyard each year as harvest approaches. Together, the two images relate a narrative of renewal. That narrative extends to the viticulture. Its vineyards tended through regenerative practices, Beyond Shadows makes the case for a living vineyard ecosystem. Rather than treating vineyards as a resource to be exploited, Doña Paula is embracing a cycle of life, death and renewal. It is a natural balance that should not be avoided; the label represents the idea that life and death are bound in the vineyard. In making the wine, Doña Paula has drawn on the sense of balance to pay tribute to its high-elevation vineyards in Luján de Cuyo. The winemaking philosophy balances tradition and innovation, with gentle handling and careful extraction echoing the care taken in the regeneratively-farmed vineyards. Each step blends historical reverennce and modern technique to tell the region’s story. As one of the foremost guardians of Mendoza’s winemaking traditions, Doña Paula is using Beyond Shadows to tell the story of Luján de Cuyo. The wine, available in the UK through NorthSouth Wines, is a testament to the region’s history and a reminder of its potential still to be revealed.

title: RNDC court filings reveal scale of distributor’s financial collapse
summary:
Court documents filed following Republic National Distributing Company's Chapter 11 bankruptcy have revealed more than US$400 million in unsecured debts and mounting financial pressures stretching back several years. The filings also raise fresh questions about whether major suppliers recognised the distributor's deteriorating position before ending their partnerships.

The post RNDC court filings reveal scale of distributor’s financial collapse appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Court documents filed following Republic National Distributing Company's Chapter 11 bankruptcy have revealed more than US$400 million in unsecured debts and mounting financial pressures stretching back several years. The filings also raise fresh questions about whether major suppliers recognised the distributor's deteriorating position before ending their partnerships. The full impact of Republic National Distributing Company's collapse into Chapter 11 bankruptcy has been revealed in court documents scrutinised by the Lexington Herald, which closely follows the US spirits industry. The immediate conclusion is that America's second-largest drinks distributor had been sinking deeper into financial difficulty for several years, but it was the Covid pandemic and its aftermath that ultimately triggered its collapse. Overall, RNDC has around 100,000 unsecured creditors to whom it owes more than US$400 million. Many of the smaller creditors are vulnerable to being pushed into financial difficulty themselves, as they are unlikely to absorb the expected losses.

Biggest debts revealed

The largest single debt, almost US$94 million, is owed to Proximo, the US supplier of Jose Cuervo tequila, which is ultimately controlled by Mexico's largest spirits producer, Becle. Others in line for what may prove to be limited debt recovery include Delicato Family Wines, which is owed US$14.4 million, Anheuser-Busch (US$4.7 million), Pernod Ricard (US$4 million) and Gallo (US$1.8 million). Meanwhile, Scotch whisky producer Edrington, owner of The Macallan and Highland Park, is owed US$4.7 million. Business unravelled before bankruptcy As previously reported by the drinks business, RNDC began dismantling significant parts of its business following its withdrawal from California in September 2025 after losing major supplier accounts including Brown-Forman and Tito's. After entering Chapter 11 protection, the company also confirmed to the drinks business that prospective buyers had already expressed interest in acquiring parts of its remaining operations as it pursued an orderly wind-down of the business. In January, the company agreed terms to sell operations in Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, South Carolina, Virginia and Washington, DC, to Reyes Beverage Group. It had lost several high-profile supplier relationships over the previous two years, including Brown-Forman, Pernod Ricard and Treasury Wine Estates, as major producers increasingly reconsidered their distribution strategies.

Did suppliers see the warning signs?

The key question, however, is whether those companies changed their distribution strategies because they realised RNDC was already in financial trouble. The company's sales topped US$12 billion in 2022 as the post-Covid boom gathered pace. They then fell by almost 10% in 2023 as the temporary surge in demand reversed amid inflationary pressures and weaker consumer spending. Court filings suggest RNDC had become locked into purchasing agreements that appeared highly attractive when demand was soaring but later forced the company to buy far more stock than it could sell as the market weakened. The result was a substantial inventory overhang.

Suppliers tightened terms

Sazerac alleges RNDC had been experiencing financial problems since at least 2021, when the two companies renegotiated their agreement. According to Sazerac, within six months RNDC had begun failing to pay invoices. The company also claims that, in 2023, RNDC required customers to purchase less sought-after products in order to gain access to highly sought-after brands such as Pappy Van Winkle. According to bankruptcy court filings, RNDC lost suppliers "that together accounted for more than US$3 billion in annual revenue" in less than three years. As producers departed in large numbers, those that remained "began extracting more onerous contractual terms ... renewal of one of the company's key contracts resulted in an approximate US$50 million reduction in gross profit simply for re-signing the contract," the court documents state. Meanwhile, competitors sought to increase market share by offering "aggressive, more favourable terms ... which intensified margin compression across the entire industry," according to the filings.

What happens next?

RNDC says it has reached agreements to sell its remaining assets as going concerns and wind down its remaining operations over the coming months. How much unsecured creditors will ultimately recover, however, remains an open question.

title: Bordeaux revives ‘Claret’ for new generation of drinkers
summary:
Bordeaux is revamping ‘claret’ for a modern wine-drinking audience, with an emphasis on light, low-tannin and unoaked wines destined for the fridge. Patrick Schmitt MW considers the facts.

The post Bordeaux revives ‘Claret’ for new generation of drinkers appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Bordeaux is revamping ‘claret’ for a modern wine-drinking audience, with an emphasis on light, low-tannin and unoaked wines destined for the fridge. Patrick Schmitt MW considers the facts.

The world’s most famous wine region, and the benchmark for high-end Cabernets and Merlots, Bordeaux is reviving its historic ‘claret’ name as the banner for a new category of light, fruit-forward, chillable dry red wines aimed at attracting younger consumers back to region. The initiative, led by the Syndicat des AOC Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur, follows a 2023 consultation prompted by falling red wine consumption and an ageing consumer base. Managing director of the Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur Wine Union Stéphanie Sinoquet told the drinks business that the decision was informed by consumer research and product testing across six priority markets: the UK, France, Belgium, Germany, China and Japan. Rather than creating a new appellation, the union has introduced a regulated ‘mention traditionnelle’ called Bordeaux Claret, effective from the 2025 vintage. All Bordeaux red grape varieties are permitted, although early production has relied mainly on Merlot with some Malbec. Short maceration of two to four days produces lightly coloured, low-tannin, unoaked wines intended to be served chilled.

Begins where dark rosé ends

The specification defines Claret as a ruby to light-purple, fruit-forward red with moderate intensity, ripe red fruit aromas and a structure designed for early drinking. It begins where the dark rosé ‘Bordeaux Clairet’ ends, with a minimum Colour Intensity Index (ICM) of 3, while featuring less pronounced amylic character (such as cotton candy aromatics) than you might find in Clairet. Winemaking methods remain flexible, but every wine must meet the required sensory profile through assessment by an independent tasting panel. Minimum alcohol is set at 11% ABV, with most wines expected at 12%–13%. Malolactic fermentation is optional, and, while residual sugar is capped at 3g/l for the traditional style of Bordeaux, the cap is raised to 7g/l for the chillable expression. A minimum grape sugar level of 189g/l at harvest is also required to ensure sufficient fruit ripeness. De-alcoholisation is not permitted under PDO rules. chillable red It is recommended that producers display ‘Bordeaux Claret’ prominently on front labels, alongside descriptors such as ‘fruity’, ‘fresh’ or ‘chillable red’ to distinguish the style from traditional claret. Wines failing to meet the specification cannot use the designation.

Big Bordeaux brands on board

The first vintage has already exceeded expectations, with around 16,500 hectolitres – roughly two million bottles – produced by about 40 wineries. Importantly, participation extends beyond small estates to major négociants and brands including Calvet and Mouton Cadet. The marketing strategy is focused firmly on the on-trade, with by-the-glass service, including over ice, seen as the best way to build consumer awareness. Recommended serving temperature is around 5°C, although the wines are intended to perform well up to 10°C–12°C. Promotional activity will initially target France, Belgium, Germany and the UK through trade events and media, rather than consumer advertising. In the UK specifically, a small group of buyers for London merchants are reluctant to lose the term ‘claret’ for traditional red Bordeaux, encouraging the wine growers union to emphasise the broader “chillable red” category in its messaging. Outside the UK, claret doesn’t carry the same fame and association. The relaunch has prompted discussion within Bordeaux over whether the claret designation should eventually be shared more widely across France, although any change would require a formal vote. The launch comes as Bordeaux continues to contract its vineyard area following years of oversupply. Regional vineyard area has fallen sharply since 2021 through uprooting and reclassification, providing the backdrop against which Bordeaux Claret’s commercial performance will be judged.

The background

  • 'Claret' is not a new invention: it was the name given by English merchants to the lighter-coloured Bordeaux wines exported after the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry II in 1152.
  • While 'claret' became the generic British term for Bordeaux red, Bordeaux is now reclaiming the word to define a specific modern wine style.

The launch

  • Bordeaux Claret is a new regulated category introduced under the Bordeaux AOC as a mention traditionnelle (traditional designation), rather than a new appellation. It applies from the 2025 vintage.
  • The initiative was officially unveiled at Wine Paris 2026 after a fast-tracked approval process with France's wine regulator, the INAO.

The wine style

  • Light-coloured ruby red
  • Fruit-driven with soft tannins
  • Unoaked
  • Intended to be served chilled
  • Designed for early drinking rather than cellaring
  • Sits stylistically between traditional Bordeaux red and Bordeaux Clairet

Production rules

  • All Bordeaux red varieties are permitted
  • Merlot is expected to dominate early releases
  • Short maceration produces lower colour and tannin
  • Wines must pass an independent tasting panel
  • Minimum 11% ABV
  • Residual sugar up to 7g/l
  • De-alcoholisation is prohibited

Commercial rollout

  • Around 40 producers have already made Bordeaux Claret
  • The first vintage totals roughly 16,500hl (around two million bottles)
  • Participants include major brands such as Mouton Cadet and Calvet, suggesting broad industry backing rather than a niche experiment

Marketing strategy

  • Focus is on restaurants and bars rather than retail
  • Promotion centres on by-the-glass service
  • Wines are recommended served around 5°C (and remain suitable up to 10-12°C)
  • Marketing emphasises descriptors such as "fresh", "fruity" and "chillable red"

title: Bibi Graetz reflects on leaving La Place de Bordeaux
summary:
On a recent visit to Tuscany, db's Bordeaux correspondent, Colin Hay talked to Bibi Graetz about his decision to leave La place de Bordeaux and his ambition, which has always been "to make better and better wines". 

The post Bibi Graetz reflects on leaving La Place de Bordeaux appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: On a recent visit to Tuscany, db's Bordeaux correspondent, Colin Hay talked to Bibi Graetz about his decision to leave La place de Bordeaux and his ambition, which has always been "to make better and better wines".  It is hardly a jealously guarded secret that the world of fine wine is today in crisis. And crisis is an accelerator of change. One symptom of that change is the rapid evolution of La Place de Bordeaux, notably with respect to its offering of wines from beyond Bordeaux itself. I took the opportunity of a recent trip to Florence to visit one of La Place’s most iconic of ‘hors Bordeaux’ stars, Bibi Graetz. From his tasting room perch in Fiesole, overlooking the city below, we talked about his almost immediate success on La Place de Bordeaux and his painful and difficult decision to leave it last year. Below is a simple précis of our conversation. Given the sensitivity and importance of many of the issues we discussed I offer no analysis here of the implications of his comments (that is for later) and I prefer to leave Bibi’s thoughts in his own words. But I would like to record my extreme gratitude to him for sharing with us his reflections on what is undoubtedly a painful episode with much wider implications for La Place and the world of fine wine today. Describe to us your history with La Place. How did it all begin?  I had been thinking at La Place already for many years but couldn’t find an entry route. Suddenly, in 2018, I found an open window and I jumped. I met a négociant at the first Tuscany en primeur tasting of James Suckling, and we became partners and good friends. What made this such a success from the start? I was super creative and was coming with new and fresh ideas all the time. And very fast, it became a huge success, probably one of the greatest ‘beyond Bordeaux’ success stories. In three years, the brand exploded, and we established Testamatta and Colore on the global fine wine scene. These wines attained a whole new level of worldwide recognition which we are very proud of still today. It has been so much fun, and everybody was a bit ‘drunk’ from this incredible success; we really loved it all. So what went wrong?  In 2023 something changed. I came in Bordeaux in August, just before the September release, and one of my closest négociant friends told me: ‘Bibi the situation is dramatic!’. He said: ‘the only phrase I have to describe it is … FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS, this is going to be difficult …. And what we are seeing now is not the bottom, it is only going to get worse!’. Things has already started slowing down and by the time we arrived at the release of the 2023 vintage in September 2025 the négociants were under financial pressure. They wanted to act as agents and not as négociants anymore, buying only what, in effect, they had already sold. The result was that they could not commit to the vintage, or at least not for the ‘beyond Bordeaux’ wines like ours. We told them that without commitment we would leave … The rest, as they say, is history!  The reaction from our partners was really fast. They took the opportunity, stepped back in and committed where the négociants of La Place would not.  How does that decision feel today? And what does the future hold for you? With La Place de Bordeaux, we reached heights that I had never thought possible in my wildest dreams. So we are sorry that we were obliged to leave. But, on the other hand, we are thankful for the opportunity, all we did together and for what we achieved with La Place. Now our focus is on maintaining what we have built. We believe that nowadays exclusive distribution is the best way to go. We have a very strong brand and that is a blessing in today’s complicated global market situation. Our drive has always been to make better and better wines. Consistent with that, from the 2022 vintage onwards, all our wine will come from vineyards above 400 metres. That reduces significantly our overall production whilst bringing a whole new dimension to our wines, with incredible parfums, freshness and acidity.

title: Australians brace for alcohol tax hike blow
summary:
From Monday, tax on RTDs and spirits is set to leap to AU$110.15 per litre in Australia in what is one of the largest six-month increases outside of Covid. 

The post Australians brace for alcohol tax hike blow appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
From Monday, tax on RTDs and spirits is set to leap to AU$110.15 per litre in Australia in what is one of the largest six-month increases outside of Covid.  Australians are bracing to pay more for spirits and packaged beer, as the Australian federal government imposes its 79th alcohol tax hike in 40 years.  Australian brewers and distillers now pay the third highest tax rate in the world – only surpassed by several countries in Scandinavia – with the government preparing to cash in AU$9.1bn in total alcohol taxes this year. For a standard 700ml bottle of spirits, approximately $30 of the retail price is alcohol excise before GST is applied.  The twice-yearly automatic indexation was introduced by the Hawke Government in 1983, led by treasurer at the time Paul Keating.  But experts warn that the system is now encouraging a surge in demand for cheap, bootleg alcohol alternatives This follows research showing taxed spirits are becoming unaffordable, leading to soaring drink costs and demand for cheap, bootleg alternatives, with illicit alcohol now making up a 7.5% slice of total Australian alcohol by volume, with this figure even higher for bottled spirits.

'Driving demand'  for illicit alcohol

Steven Fanner, who became executive director of Spirits & Cocktails Australia last year, said: “We have a system where twice-yearly tax hikes on alcohol have been on auto-pilot since the early 1980s. “This means that from next week the tax on spirits is now over $110 per litre of pure alcohol – a rate six times higher than the United States and about double New Zealand. “This is not a system that should be a set-and-forget — without reform the government risks a myriad of unintended consequences, including driving demand for cheap, black-market alternatives.” However, others have embraced the hikes. Speaking to 7News, Nicole Lee, CEO of Hello Sunday Morning, said: “There’s absolutely no doubt that increasing the excise helps reduce public health problems.”

Draught beer and wine dodge the hike

Draught beer is exempt from the biannual hikes, as part of the two-year tax holiday that commenced in August 2025.  When it first came into force, the draught beer tax freeze marked the first time either the spirits or beer tax remained level since automatic indexation was introduced. Since then the spirits sector has called for an extension to include draught spirits, but this was vetoed by the Senate.  Wine, too, is not impacted by the hikes, as it is subject to a separate tax system.

title: Draught beer is about to get more expensive in South Korea – here’s why
summary:
From the end of this year, South Korea will slash the 20% tax break on draught beer, the government has announced in the 2026 tax reform plan, with bars across the country bracing for cost increases. 

The post Draught beer is about to get more expensive in South Korea – here’s why appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
From the end of this year, South Korea will slash the 20% tax break on draught beer, the government has announced in the 2026 tax reform plan, with bars across the country bracing for cost increases.  Bars and restaurants across South Korea are steeling themselves  for price hikes after the government announced that the 20% tax holiday on draught beer will end from next year, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy’s 2026 tax reform package.  Currently, beer taxes are decided on volume instead of price. While standard beer is taxed at 885,700 won per kilolitre, the tax rate for draught beer is 708,560 – thanks to the 20% discount the category has been subject to since 2020. Six years ago, the government issued the 20% tax holiday in a bid to help the draught beer industry, whose tax burden had grown disproportionately large, and the application period has since been extended multiple times. However, officials have now decided that the beer sector has sufficiently benefited from the reduction, prompting the decision to end it later this year. From 2027, the tax burden per glass is projected to rise by about 130 won, with the tax rates for draught beer lifting to come in line with regular beer. This will see the tax burden for draught beer increase by 177,140 won per kilolitre. 

The burden on Korea's bars

When education tax and value-added tax is taken into account, the tax burden at the shipment stage is expected to soar by more than 200,000 won per kilolitre. Converted to a single 20-litre keg of draught beer used by ordinary establishments, the tax adds about 5,000 won more, translating to around 130 won per 500ml glass for consumers. While this may not seem like much per glass, the accumulated amount can grow significantly for larger venues with high sales volumes. Korea’s hospitality sector, which is already grappling with surging costs of labour, rent and raw materials, is  worried that the draught beer price hikes will lead to higher costs for the consumer. 

Venues close as Koreans cut back on booze

Over the past eight years, nearly half of Korea’s pubs have shut for good. Figures released by the National Tax Service (NTS) show that the number of casual pubs and beer houses nationwide fell to 28,178 in March 2026, down from 52,302 when records were first compiled in 2018. The decline means more than 24,000 establishments have disappeared, representing a 46% contraction in the sector. Casual pubs, known locally as ganee jujeom, recorded a 10.2% annual decline, falling from 8,894 to 7,985 businesses. Beer-focused establishments, or hof pubs, dropped by 9.4% over the same period, from 22,282 to 20,193.  Years of elevated inflation have increased rents, labour expenses and operating costs, placing pressure on small independent businesses that dominate South Korea’s pub sector. At the same time, traditional after-work drinking gatherings which were once a staple of corporate culture, have become less common, with consumers drinking less across the board.  The proof is in the numbers, with South Korea’s household alcohol spend seeing its sharpest drop in seven years in the first quarter of 2026. Traditionally, quarters containing the Lunar New Year or Chuseok holidays have seen alcohol purchases surge, but even these periods have now seen sales slip as alcohol sales dry up.

A regional picture

This is reflective of a broader regional trend, as consumers cut back on alcohol across the Asia Pacific region. Last year, three in 10 APAC consumers said they were drinking less alcohol in 2025 versus the prior year, according to data from NielsenIQ.  “APAC consumers are no longer drinking out of habit — they’re drinking with purpose,” James Phillips, head of beverage alcohol APAC at NielsenIQ, previously told the drinks business. He added: “The shift toward mindful consumption is not a passing trend, but a cultural reset that’s redefining how, when and why people drink. The key question – is this the new normal in the on-premise?  “If so, it presents big challenges for suppliers, manufacturers and operators, including the need to cater for moderating guests without alienating core consumers.  “Brands that can gain a deep understanding of this complex recalibration and adapt nimbly will be the ones that stay relevant in the months and years ahead.”

title: Why Woodforde’s has chosen to ‘celebrate the brewery’s Norfolk roots’
summary:
Woodforde’s Brewery has revealed new keg branding to match the business’s established cask presence in pubs and bars. But there is one extra reminder for its customers - Norfolk is where you can find great beer. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Why Woodforde’s has chosen to ‘celebrate the brewery’s Norfolk roots’ appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Woodforde’s Brewery has revealed new keg branding to match the business’s established cask presence in pubs and bars. But there is one extra reminder for its customers - Norfolk is where you can find great beer. Jessica Mason reports. The Broadland-based brewery’s new look was applied across its entire keg range from  Norfolk Day (27 July) and included on keg lenses and glassware for pubs stocking its beers. As part of the rebrand, Woodforde’s will see its English Lager renamed as Woodforde’s Lager and Volt 0.5 will be named Woodforde’s 0.5 and, according to the company, the change celebrates the brewery’s Norfolk roots, with nods to local landmarks such as Norwich Cathedral, natural beauty spots and the famous Wherry boats which gave their name to Woodforde’s first ever beer. The beer sector is also in agreement in unison that Norfolk and specifically Norwich, is synonymous with historic beer and pub landmarks that are admired all over the world.

'Beautiful' and 'walkable'

Speaking to the drinks business, Woodforde’s CEO Paul Sullivan said: "Rewind to the days before Woodforde's formation in 1981 and Norfolk had lost its reputation for great beer, as national giants bought out and closed the county's breweries, starving local people of a pint they could be proud of. That's why Woodforde's was born." Sullivan explained to db that "Norfolk and its fields are home to world-famous malts, helping our beers stand out among the crowd as a real crowd pleaser. It's also home to some of the country's oldest and best pubs, something we should all be fiercely proud of." Describing Norwich, Varvar Brewery spokesperson, beer judge and Ukraine's first certified cicerone, Lana Svitankova also told db: "I don't know any other city having a pub where you can get a dark mild 10 out of 10 visits. All in all, it's beautiful, it's walkable, and the number of excellent places offering both cask and modern beer is plenty." Sullivan, said: “These simple yet captivating designs will fit in seamlessly with the competitors on the bar – they stand out for all the right reasons. We remain committed to our cask roots and our multi-award-winning range of traditional ales, but it was about time we brought our keg products into a uniform range.” World Beer Awards judge Mick Dore told db: "Norwich is one of Britain's finest beer cities. Built on beer, defined by its regional brews, where beer belongs and brewing leads."

Connecting with customers looking for quality

Sullivan explained that the Woodforde’s “name is synonymous with quality – and this new look with our name proudly at the centre will only create further trust and connection with customers looking for a quality pint, whether that’s cask, keg, bottle or can”. The relaunch follows the brewery having released its latest foray into the pale ale market, Woodforde’s Pale Ale, at this year’s Royal Norfolk Show. The 4% vegan and gluten free beer was also brewed as a celebration of Nelson’s County and proved a hit at this year’s show – with customers queuing at the bar to get their hands on the first pints.

Perfectly capturing Norfolk's splendour

Woodforde’s Pale Ale, alongside other beers in the brewery’s extensive range of keg products, will be served in the new-look glasses, while its range of canned beers will also feature Norfolk-themed artwork. Sullivan admitted: “We’ve listened to what our customers want – they don’t just want us to be the Taste of Norfolk, they want us to champion our magnificent home county and bask in the glory of our beautiful Broadland home. It has been a joy working alongside local illustrator Owen Mathers on the designs who has perfectly captured the splendour of our beautiful county – they would certainly make me want to visit. Every keg lens and glass shows exactly who we are – a brewery proud of our heritage serving up quality beer.” He added: "That's what we're all about here at Woodforde's – being the Taste of Norfolk. We champion local ingredients and the producers behind them – and our new keg branding ensures that message of love for all things Norfolk is at the forefront." Pubs looking to stock Woodforde’s keg range can contact the brewery.

title: Chateau Denmark Hill: “We’re hoping for 22 bottles this year, but we’re not allowed to sell it.”
summary:
Following the news that south London train station Denmark Hill is producing its first vintage of Bacchus, Sarah Neish speaks to the project's winemakers about staying on track and not going loco in the British heatwave.

The post Chateau Denmark Hill: “We’re hoping for 22 bottles this year, but we’re not allowed to sell it.” appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Following the news that south London train station Denmark Hill is producing its first vintage of Bacchus, Sarah Neish speaks to the project's winemakers about staying on track and not going loco in the British heatwave.   As db reported yesterday, the UK's first railway station wine is well underway with the inaugural vintage from 'Chateau Denmark Hill' expected to be ready to drink next year. We caught up Nick Mair, co-winemaker for the south London project alongside Tony Coleman, to find out the triumphs and tribulations of growing vines just metres away from the train tracks. According to Nair, vibrations from trains passing at speed are "not an issue". "The vineyard is well above the tracks," he said. "Had it been at the same level we would have been more worried. The vines appear to be flourishing and rose bushes at the ends of each row bloom prodigiously. Plus, the prevailing wind is south westerly which then tends to run east along the tracks."

Winning formula

Intriguingly, neither Mair, nor Coleman, have had a career in wine, "though we are keen wine drinkers", Mair tells db. Rather, Coleman works in construction while Mair is a French and Spanish language teacher. The combination has proved to be a winning formula. "I tend to have ideas but Tony has the perseverance and construction background, without which the vineyard wouldn’t have happened," said Mair. That vineyard comprises 30 vines of aromatic white grape variety Bacchus, located within Denmark Hill train station's grounds in Camberwell. After Network Rail granted a special Community License to the Camberwell Society, of which Mair and Coleman are members, efforts were made to "clean up" the station and surrounding area. In Mair's words, the station "was one of the dodgier parts of Camberwell - a reputation we wanted to change. It was strewn with litter and we wanted to make it somewhere special." Along with installing various artworks and gardening projects, including a mini lavender farm, the Bacchus vines were planted as a way of helping the local community and commuters  to"engage more positively with the station," said Nair. It's all part of what he calls "the Provencification of Camberwell."

Forgiving variety

Bacchus was chosen by the novice winegrowers because Nair and Coleman, running point on the project, had noted that the variety was "successfully widely grown in South East England", and perhaps most importantly, is "forgiving for beginners!" However, before leaping straight in, the pair started off with another crop entirely. "I planted sunflowers in 2022 just to check [the soil's viability]," said Nair. "The horizon is very low and the vineyard is due south. We also checked soil records with Network Rail. Encouraged by a bumper sunflower crop, we removed bindweed in the autumn of 2023, terraced the ground and then augured in vertical posts, which was very hard work as we had no electricity or mechanical agricultural equipment." Thankfully, this is where Coleman's background in construction came into its own, meaning "we were able to make accurate plans to ensure an appropriate build, dig and structure" for the vineyard site. It hasn't all been sunshine and roses (or indeed sunflowers), with manpower a continual issue, especially for tending the vines.  At the start, Nair said, "we asked for volunteers who were prepared to help with the hard labour — we were honest about the scale of the project — and plenty wanted to dig in the vines, but nothing else."

New skills

While the team was short on professional winemaking experience, Nair had plenty of travel to winemaking regions under his belt, where he had picked up a thing or two. "As a French and Spanish teacher, I have spent some years in those countries," he said, adding that "part of the  A-level syllabus also used to allow for the study of a region – and 15 years of school trips to Jerez, including research interviews" not only helped him to "appreciate a good fino Sherry" but also to learn about the making and bottling of wines. He also spent a year in Cahors in the south of France, and time in the Alpes-Maritimes. Meanwhile, Coleman embarked on a vine-tending course at The Mount Vineyard in Shoreham, Kent, where he made the call to prune the Denmark Hill vines using the double Guyot method. According to Nair, "2026 will be the station's first proper harvest and the grapes are looking good - though a little rain at some stage would be helpful!" He of course refers to the unprecedented British summer heatwave, where the temperature has scarcely dipped below 30°C for months. Regarding the expected yield he revealed that the pair have pruned back to "something like nine bunches per vine" and given that the pair are beginners "we would be happy with 22 bottles in a first year – so a bottle per vine."

Not for sale

As the Camberwell Society "has an understanding with Network Rail that we will not sell any wine," interested parties will sadly not be able to purchase a bottle of Chateau Denmark Hill. At least for the timebeing. "It's really a passion project," said Nair, who has received advice, support and encouragement from various parties. "We have found it to be a very welcoming community, from growers to Masters of Wines, and independent local wine shops." "Given the excellence of English winemaking we are clearly enthusiasts rather than experienced viticulturists," he said. "Sip it and see will be our approach!" Are there plans to scale up the vineyard in the future? "There's not much available land in Camberwell," Nair quipped. However, when one is bitten by the winemaking bug, one tends to find a way, and the pair's next project might just take them further off the beaten tracks...

title: Campari profits fall despite stronger outlook for 2026
summary:
Davide Campari-Milano reported lower first-half profits despite delivering organic sales growth and improving earnings. The spirits group also upgraded its full-year margin outlook, citing a more favourable tariff environment and continued progress in streamlining its portfolio.

The post Campari profits fall despite stronger outlook for 2026 appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Davide Campari-Milano reported lower first-half profits despite delivering organic sales growth and improving earnings. The spirits group also upgraded its full-year margin outlook, citing a more favourable tariff environment and continued progress in streamlining its portfolio. Davide Campari-Milano, the parent company of Campari and Aperol, saw its first-half 2026 profits decline, although its overall results were encouraging. Net profit for the period was €129 million, down from €206 million in the first six months of 2025. Net sales fell by 1.0% on a reported basis to €1.51 billion from €1.53 billion in 2025, reflecting the effect of portfolio disposals and foreign exchange movements. On an organic basis, net sales increased by 2.7%. Adjusted pre-tax earnings rose by 1.8% on a reported basis to €358 million from €352 million, while adjusted net profit increased by 4.7% to €226 million.

Tariff outlook improves

Looking ahead, the company raised its outlook for its full-year adjusted earnings margin due to what it believes is an improved tariff environment. The group now expects the full-year negative effect of tariffs to be €20 million, down from its previous forecast of €30 million.

Strategy gains momentum

Chief executive Simon Hunt said: "We are delivering on our strategy and growing with solid results in the first half of 2026 in terms of organic topline, profitability and a solid balance sheet. "At the same time, we are growing and gaining share across all our key markets, driven by our priority brands. "Our strategy of fewer bigger bets, including the disposal of non-priority brands, innovation and geographic expansion, is gaining traction while we continue to drive efficiency across each line of the P&L."

Portfolio reshaping continues

As part of its brand disposal programme, Campari is selling Bisquit & Dubouché Cognac and Cabo Wabo tequila to Cobblestone Brands, alongside a separate agreement to sell the Caribbean rum business of Bellonnie et Bourdillon Successeurs to a French private industry player.

title: Semaglutide cuts heavy drinking days in small alcohol trial
summary:
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in the in-demand diabetes drug Ozempic, reduced heavy drinking days and alcohol-related harm in a phase 2 clinical trial of people with alcohol use disorder.

The post Semaglutide cuts heavy drinking days in small alcohol trial appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in the in-demand diabetes drug Ozempic, reduced heavy drinking days and alcohol-related harm in a phase 2 clinical trial of people with alcohol use disorder. An oral form of semaglutide significantly reduced heavy drinking days among adults seeking treatment for alcohol use disorder, although it did not meet the study’s primary endpoint for laboratory-assessed craving. Researchers said the mixed results support larger trials rather than establishing the drug as a treatment. An oral form of semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days, alcohol-related harm and everyday cravings in a small clinical trial involving people with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder. The phase 2 study, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry, enrolled 50 treatment-seeking adults and compared daily oral semaglutide with a placebo over eight weeks. Participants received 3mg of semaglutide each day for four weeks, followed by 7mg daily for the remaining four weeks. The researchers found that semaglutide significantly reduced the number of heavy drinking days compared with placebo. Participants taking the drug also consumed fewer drinks on the days when they drank. However, semaglutide did not significantly reduce the study’s primary outcome, alcohol craving measured in a laboratory after participants were exposed to their preferred drink. It also failed to produce a statistically significant reduction in the average number of drinks consumed per calendar day.

Fewer heavy drinking days

During the final four weeks of treatment, participants receiving semaglutide recorded significantly fewer heavy drinking days than those taking the placebo. The drug also reduced drinks per drinking day, naturalistic alcohol cravings reported outside the laboratory and alcohol-related negative consequences. More people in the semaglutide group reduced their World Health Organisation risk drinking level by at least one category. Cannabis use days also declined among the small group of participants who reported using cannabis before the study, although this was an exploratory finding rather than one of the trial’s principal outcomes. The authors concluded that the results support continued investigation of semaglutide as a possible treatment for alcohol use disorder.

Primary endpoint missed

Despite the reductions in several drinking measures, the trial did not find a significant difference between semaglutide and placebo in cue-induced craving at week six. Participants were asked to hold and smell their preferred alcoholic drink for three minutes before rating the strength of their craving. The scores did not differ significantly between the two groups. The researchers also found no statistically significant reduction in drinks per calendar day during the final four weeks, although the result approached the study’s significance threshold. The findings therefore present a more qualified picture than reports suggesting GLP-1 medicines simply remove the desire to drink.

Early evidence

Interest in drugs such as semaglutide has grown following anecdotal reports from patients using GLP-1 receptor agonists for diabetes or weight management who said their interest in alcohol had diminished. Animal studies and observational research have also suggested that the medicines may influence reward pathways involved in alcohol consumption. A previous trial of injectable semaglutide involving people with less severe alcohol use disorder who were not seeking treatment found reductions in heavy drinking days, drinks per drinking day and craving. The latest trial tested an oral formulation among people actively seeking help and experiencing more severe alcohol problems. Researchers said oral treatment may prove attractive to patients who would prefer a tablet to a weekly injection.

Small trial requires caution

The study was conducted at a single US academic centre between November 2023 and October 2025 and included only 50 participants, all of whom had a body mass index of at least 25. Of those enrolled, 47 completed the eight-week treatment period. Three participants withdrew from the semaglutide group, including one who experienced an allergic reaction considered probably related to the medication. The authors acknowledged the trial’s moderate sample size and exploratory nature. No adjustment was made for testing multiple secondary outcomes, which means some positive findings require confirmation in larger studies. Semaglutide is not currently approved as a treatment for alcohol use disorder. The US Food and Drug Administration has approved three medications for the condition, which the researchers described as only modestly effective.

title: Is wine good for you? Here’s what the evidence says
summary:
Between WHO warnings and NHS guidelines lies a complex truth about wine, health and why humans have never stopped drinking it. Gabriel Stone considers the effect of booze on your body. 

The post Is wine good for you? Here’s what the evidence says appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Between WHO warnings and NHS guidelines lies a complex truth about wine, health and why humans have never stopped drinking it. Gabriel Stone considers the effect of booze on your body. Is wine good for you? Alcohol and calories are what most people have in mind when they ask this question so let’s start – but certainly not finish – there. If you’re looking to lose weight, then cutting back on the amount of wine you drink is an obvious step. Official guidance on the UK’s National Health Service website suggests that a standard 175ml glass of 12% ABV wine will contain “up to” 158 calories. That’s fewer than you’ll find in a pint of 5% ABV beer but more calorific than a 50ml measure of 40% ABV spirits or even a 330ml can of standard Coca-Cola. Alcohol makes a considerable contribution to this tally, packing in 7 calories per gram. The higher a wine’s alcohol content, the more calories your glass will contain. But don’t assume that zero alcohol equals zero calories. Low/no-alcohol wines often compensate with relatively high levels of residual sugar at 4 calories per gram. To pick a market leading example from the booming non-alcoholic wine category, sparkling fizz Nozeco contains about 50 calories in a 175ml serve.

Abstinence or a healthy balance

If your concerns are more about alcohol’s intoxicating properties then here non-alcoholic wine – or indeed any other alcohol-free beverage – does present a clear cut solution. For most wine lovers though, the objective is not abstinence but rather to strike a healthy balance. Some experts would suggest there’s no such thing. Read the World Health Organisation’s guidance and you might conclude that a Friday night glass of Chablis simply isn’t worth the risk. At the top of its charge sheet comes the warning that “alcohol is a toxic, psychoactive, and dependence-producing substance and has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer decades ago – this is the highest risk group, which also includes asbestos, radiation and tobacco.” For now, at least, the NHS takes a more measured view. It advises both men and women “not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis. That translates to roughly six pints of “average-strength” beer or 10 “small glasses of lower-strength wine.”

Alcohol tolerance varies

On top of this very general guidance, consider your own body’s reaction to alcohol. Larger, leaner bodies tend to absorb it more efficiently than smaller, fatter ones. Just as unfairly, not all livers are created equal when it comes to the aldehyde dehydrogenase enzymes that break down alcohol, while some nervous systems respond in a more negative way to alcohol’s properties as a depressant. Yet while we should respect wine’s chemical make-up, it’s important to push back against the arguments of those who would reduce this drink to purely molecular evaluation. Wine is, after all, a cornerstone of the famously healthy Mediterranean diet. In fact, its consumption in the context of a meal with friends or family represents a uniquely human form of pleasure, arguably even a marker of civilisation. As both a winemaker and medical doctor, Laura Catena is particularly well-placed to fight wine’s corner as a force for good, whether through a cardiovascular or social lens. Frustrated by the rise of anti-alcohol rhetoric, she created a website In Defense of Wine to present her own considered letters and presentations on the subject of wine and health.

The benefits of moderation

“As a physician and scientist, I believe there is not enough proof to impose ‘no safe limit for alcohol consumption’ as a general health policy directive,” Catena argues. “Many studies in reputable, peer-reviewed journals have shown that those who drink in moderation tend to have lower all-cause mortality. Moreover, the pleasure and conviviality of moderate alcohol consumption should not be dismissed without robust evidence of its harm. I urge individuals to make their own alcohol consumption decisions in consultation with a doctor.” Humans have wrestled for generations with the question of how, or indeed whether, society can safely navigate this complex relationship with fermented grape juice. Politicians today would do well to recall Euripides’ 5th century BC tragedy The Bacchae, where state prohibition is associated with prurience, and authoritarian rejection of the wine god Dionysos results in disaster.

Whoever drinks good wine, sees God

Perhaps the most influential advocate for wine as a force for good in recent millennia is Christianity. The Cistercian monastic order has combined centuries of theological and vinicultural studies to conclude: “Qui bon vin boit, Dieu voit” [Whoever drinks good wine, sees God]. It’s a view that chimes with the modern, secular call for quality over quantity. Here in the 21st century, the late philosopher Roger Scruton dedicated an entire book, I Drink Therefore I Am, to his argument that wine consumption is a virtue to be carefully cultivated. In short, when we weigh up whether wine is good for us, we shake a complex cocktail of the physical, mental, social and spiritual. Read on to see the nutritional composition of wine from a previous article on thedrinksbusiness.com on the possible weight loss benefits of moderate wine drinking.

The nutritional composition of wine:

  • Energy: 85kcal/100g or 125kcal/serving
  • 86% water
  • 11% alcohol
  • 2.6% carbohydrate
  • 0.1% protein

Wine – minerals

  • Total: 174.6 mg/100g
  • Potassium: 127 mg/100g
  • Phosphorus: 23 mg/100g
  • Magnesium: 12 mg/100g
  • Calcium: 8 mg/100g
  • Sodium: 4 mg/100g
  • Vitamins: 0.3 mg/100g
  • Niacin: 0.2 mg/100g
Source: National Nutrient Database for Standard Reference Release 27 of the USDA

Wine – minor components

  • Glycerol: 1%
  • Organic acids: 0.4% (mainly tartaric acid)
  • Polyphenols: 0.1%
  • Other components: 0.5% (amino acids, volatiles, acetaldehyde, higher alcohols, sorbitol, mannitol, sulfites)
Source: Professor Rosa Lamuela-Raventós

title: Could Minnesota’s THC drinks industry have been saved?
summary:
Minnesota’s THC drinks category has received a reprieve from a proposed federal ban. db looks at the details and considers how far the sector has come in a state that has been at the forefront of the trend.

The post Could Minnesota’s THC drinks industry have been saved? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Minnesota’s THC drinks category has received a reprieve from a proposed federal ban. db looks at the details and considers how far the sector has come in a state that has been at the forefront of the trend. The reprieve, which was part of a bill the US senate passed on Monday, will mean a short-term bill will fund the government until 11 December and will also delay any new federal regulations on THC drinks.

Breathing space for the sector

According to local reports via MinnPost, the new regulations would have affected Minnesota’s drinks manufacturers using cannabidiol (CBD) in a move that has had the potential to reshape the category and either help or hinder its progress across the state. THC-infused drinks are fast-becoming a growing revenue stream for struggling US craft brewers. But with shifting regulations and unclear federal policy, many producers have feared that the category could be curtailed just as it begins to transform the market. Now, the new regulations are set to begin from 11 November, giving manufacturers and loyal consumers a little breathing space prior to any rash decisions being made as the validity of the category is weighed up by senators. Meanwhile, the senate bill, which is expected to win final approval later this week, will only provide a month’s worth of respite.

A leading example of THC drinks being sold in a regulated manner

Speaking in a recent statement, senator Tina Smith said: “Adults should be allowed to have a THC beverage if they so choose. Minnesota has created one of the strongest, most carefully regulated systems in the country to allow the sale of hemp products.” Smith outlined that “the initial ban set to take place was ill-advised and would have hurt both hemp farmers and Minnesota breweries alike” since both align their business plans and staffing around the availability of the ingredient as part of the supply chain process. Minnesota in general has been a long time much-revered pioneer of the THC drinks industry after the state legalised low-potency hemp-derived THC beverages in 2022 for adults 21 and older and has thus far been heralded as an example for how the regulated sale of THC products can work in harmony with the sector. However, of late, senator Amy Klobuchar and representative Angie Craig have introduced bills that would regulate hemp beverages within the state instead of eliminating them entirely.

A delay to make a more measured and informed decision

Describing its forward moves, Klobuchar pointed out that the state of Minnesota should be used as an example for others and noted that she has made it so that “the new government funding bill in the senate includes a key provision based on my bipartisan bill to delay the federal hemp ban". Essentially, this is "so other states can put more sensible safety rules in place like we have in Minnesota". Hinting at why it was crucial to implement the bill to waylay the proceedings, Klobuchar added: “This delay was immediately necessary to give Minnesota hemp producers and customers certainty, while giving congress more time to get to a long-term fix."
